question: In the efforts to boost the EU’s energy transition – by diversifying energy sources and reducing dependence on fossil fuels – geothermal energy would appear to offer an innovative solution that could be a serious and viable prerequisite in ensuring energy diversification in the EU1. 1.
In order to support the development of geothermal energy, how will the Commission deliver on Parliament’s call for a European strategy for geothermal energy?
With this in mind, what specific measures will it put in place to encourage investment in research, development and implementation of geothermal projects at EU level?

How does it intend to integrate the geothermal dimension into the wider framework of its energy policy, ensuring that it makes a significant contribution to the EU’s goals in terms of sustainability, energy security and reducing greenhouse gas emissions?
‘EU Policy. Geothermal potential in northern, western Europe flagged as lawmakers back plan’, Euronews, 18.1.2024.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.6.2024) Over the past years, the Commission has proposed tools to support the role of geothermal energy in the wider framework of the EU’s energy system transformation, which match many of the elements in the resolution by the European Parliament.

The adoption of binding targets for renewable heating and cooling under the revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED) will be a key driver for the uptake of technologies such as geothermal heat pumps, and for further driving down their cost. RED also addresses the skills, certification and awareness bottlenecks.

The revised Energy Efficiency Directive and RED support other key drivers of geothermal energy: integrated energy planning at the local level and the accelerated decarbonisation of existing district heating and cooling systems and the development of new, renewables-based ones.

The introduction in RED of renewable energy benchmarks for the industry sector will also increase interest for innovative industrial applications of geothermal energy such as the ones highlighted in the Parliament resolution. As for the EU geothermal industry itself, the proposed Net Zero Industry Act supports future growth and competitiveness of clean energy technologies.

For geothermal industry the inclusion of lithium in the Critical Raw Materials Act will also play a key role. The challenge is now about implementation and to make sure that the available tools are used efficiently. As highlighted in the Parliament resolution, the exchange of best practices between Member States will be essential.
This in particular concerns permitting, access to geological data, financing and derisking. The Commission is actively working with national authorities to facilitate such exchanges.
